items.s: Creates brand-new shares for any investor who wants to buy, so the number of shares outstanding keeps changing.
items.w: Mutual funds make a continuous primary offering, so their share count constantly changes.

items.s: Raises capital in an initial public offering, after which the number of shares is generally fixed.
items.w: A closed-end fund’s capital structure and share count are generally fixed after its IPO.

items.s: An investor exits by redeeming shares with the issuing fund; no secondary market exists.
items.w: Mutual fund shares are redeemable only by the issuer and cannot be sold to other investors.

items.s: An investor exits by selling shares to another investor on an exchange at a market-determined price.
items.w: Closed-end shares trade investor to investor in the secondary market and are not redeemed by the fund.

items.s: May issue only common shares, never preferred stock or bonds, and cannot use leverage.
items.w: Mutual funds are limited to a single type of equity share and may not use leverage.

items.s: May issue preferred stock or bonds and borrow money to leverage its investment positions.
items.w: Closed-end funds may issue senior securities and borrow, which mutual funds cannot do.

items.s: Must calculate its net asset value at least once every business day.
items.w: Open-end funds must compute NAV daily, while closed-end funds are not required to do so.

items.s: Shares may be bought on margin or sold short because they trade on an exchange.
items.w: The comparison chart permits short selling and margin purchases only for closed-end fund shares.

title: Class A vs Class B shares

items.s: The sales charge is paid at the time of the initial purchase.
items.w: Class A shares normally carry a front-end sales charge paid when the shares are first purchased.

items.s: The sales charge is a contingent deferred charge paid only if shares are redeemed within a set number of years.
items.w: Class B shares impose a back-end CDSC when investors redeem within a specified period.

items.s: Offers breakpoint discounts for large purchases.
items.w: Class A is the share class that offers breakpoints, which discount the sales charge by dollar amount.

items.s: Does not offer breakpoints, so a large investment earns no discount on the charge.
items.w: Class B shares, like Class C, do not offer breakpoints.

items.s: Tends to carry the lowest 12b-1 fee among the share classes.
items.w: Class A typically has a lower 12b-1 fee than other share classes.

items.s: Typically imposes a 12b-1 fee that is higher than the fee on the front-end load class.
items.w: Class B shares usually charge a higher 12b-1 fee than Class A shares.

items.s: On a typical schedule the charge steps down each period and reaches zero beginning in year seven.
items.w: The typical CDSC schedule runs 5%, 4%, 3%, 3%, 2%, 1% and then 0 from year seven.

items.s: A good fit for an investor making a large purchase who wants sales charge discounts.
items.w: Large purchasers benefit from Class A breakpoints, making the front-end load worthwhile.

title: Letter of intent vs rights of accumulation

items.s: The investor signs a written promise to invest a stated total amount within 13 months.
items.w: An LOI is a contract promising a specified purchase amount over the next 13-month period.

items.s: The discount applies only to subsequent purchases, never to the initial transaction.
items.w: Under rights of accumulation the reduced sales charge is available only on later purchases.

items.s: May be backdated 90 days to reduce the sales charge on a prior purchase.
items.w: An LOI can be backdated for 90 days to lower the charge on an earlier purchase.

items.s: There is no time limit on how long the existing position may have been accumulating.
items.w: Rights of accumulation have no time limits, so old holdings still count toward the discount.

items.s: If the promised amount is not reached, extra shares held in escrow are liquidated to pay the higher sales charge.
items.w: The fund escrows the additional shares and liquidates them if the LOI is not completed.

items.s: Share appreciation and reinvested dividends may be counted when determining the value that earns the discount.
items.w: Rights of accumulation let appreciation and reinvested dividends count toward the position value.

items.s: Appreciation and reinvested dividends and capital gains do not count toward completing the commitment.
items.w: Only actual purchases count toward completing an LOI, not appreciation or reinvestments.

items.s: A position grown by market gains to just under a breakpoint earns a lower charge on the next add-on purchase.
items.w: Under rights of accumulation, appreciation can lift a position to a new breakpoint for later purchases.

items.s: Has a termination date set at the time the trust is created.
items.w: A UIT is created for a specific length of time with a termination date fixed at inception.

items.s: Has no fixed termination date.
items.w: ETFs begin with fixed portfolios but, unlike UITs, they do not have fixed termination dates.

items.s: An investor wanting out must redeem units with the trust because there is no secondary market.
items.w: UIT units are not traded in the secondary market and must be redeemed by the trust.

items.s: An investor can place a limit or stop order at midday and trade throughout the session.
items.w: ETFs are exchange-traded, so they trade intraday with the same orders used for stocks.

items.s: Administered by a trustee named in the indenture, with no board of directors or investment adviser.
items.w: UITs have a trustee and lack a board, corporate officers and investment advisers.

items.s: Its portfolio changes through reconstitution when the underlying index changes.
items.w: An ETF typically changes holdings only to mirror changes in the index it tracks.

items.s: Units of a new trust are offered only once, in the initial public offering.
items.w: A UIT sells units in an IPO and does not continuously offer new units.

items.s: Shares may be sold short or purchased on margin, and investors pay commissions.
items.w: ETFs trade like stocks, permitting short sales and margin, and they involve commissions.

items.s: Issues, redeems and cancels fund shares.
items.w: Issuing, redeeming and cancelling fund shares is a core transfer agent duty.

items.s: Holds in safekeeping all of the securities purchased for the fund’s portfolio.
items.w: The custodian is the institution that acts as caretaker of the fund’s securities.

items.s: Sends trade confirmations when fund shares are purchased or sold.
items.w: Trade confirmations to customers are a transfer agent responsibility, not a custodian task.

items.s: A bank or trust company responsible for safekeeping the fund’s assets and securities.
items.w: The Knopman Note describes the custodian as a bank or trust company safekeeping fund assets.

items.s: A shareholder missing a year-end capital gains distribution should contact this service provider.
items.w: The transfer agent handles distributing dividends and capital gains to shareholders.

items.s: Acts as caretaker of what the fund owns rather than dealing with customer transactions.
items.w: The custodian protects fund assets, while the transfer agent handles customer transactions.

items.s: Processes investor mailings and issues or cancels certificates.
items.w: The Knopman Note assigns certificates and investor mailings to the transfer agent.

items.s: Takes custody of the securities the fund buys, rather than serving customers who transact in fund shares.
items.w: The custodian safekeeps the securities purchased for the portfolio, a role distinct from customer transactions.

items.s: A rep moves a client from one fund to another with a similar objective for no legitimate investment purpose.
items.w: Switching means moving a customer between similar funds without a legitimate investment reason.

items.s: A rep sells a fund to an investor right before the fund pays out a dividend.
items.w: Selling dividends is selling a fund just ahead of its dividend payment.

items.s: Sometimes called churning because it creates extra transaction costs and possible tax liability.
items.w: Switching is referred to as churning since it adds transaction costs and potential taxes.

items.s: The payout lowers the NAV by the amount of the distribution and gives the client a taxable event.
items.w: The dividend reduces NAV and creates tax liability, so the client gains nothing real.

items.s: Liquidating one family’s growth fund to buy another family’s nearly identical growth fund is an example.
items.w: The chapter’s example is trading a Fidelity growth fund for a Janus fund with the same objectives.

items.s: The client is better off waiting to invest at the lower NAV after the dividend has been paid.
items.w: Buying after the distribution avoids the immediate tax liability on the dividend.

items.s: The violation lies in selling one fund to buy another, regardless of when dividends are paid.
items.w: Switching turns on the exchange between similar funds, not on dividend timing.

items.s: The timing of the purchase relative to the fund’s distribution is what makes the sale improper.
items.w: Selling dividends is defined by buying shortly before a distribution is paid.

items.s: The maximum is 8.5% of the POP when the fund offers all three pricing privileges.
items.w: Maximum front-end sales charge is 8.5% only if breakpoints, rights of accumulation and NAV reinvestment are offered.

items.s: The maximum is 0.75% of a fund’s average net assets for any share class.
items.w: The cap on 12b-1 fees for all mutual fund share classes is 0.75% of average net assets.

items.s: Expressed as a percentage of the public offering price, never of NAV.
items.w: A mutual fund sales load is always a percentage of the POP, not of NAV.

items.s: A fund that advertises itself as no-load may charge no more than 0.25% of average net assets.
items.w: No-load funds are limited to 12b-1 fees of 0.25% of average net assets.

items.s: Compensates the salesperson for the expertise needed to select the appropriate fund for the customer.
items.w: The sales charge pays the salesperson for expertise in choosing a suitable fund.

items.s: Covers marketing and distribution expenses but not management fees or trading expenses.
items.w: 12b-1 fees pay marketing and administrative costs, not management fees or trading costs.

items.s: A fund lacking breakpoints, rights of accumulation or NAV reinvestment is capped at 6.25% for this charge.
items.w: Funds without the three pricing features may charge a maximum sales charge of 6.25%.

items.s: Must be approved originally and annually by both shareholders and the board of directors.
items.w: A 12b-1 fee needs original and annual approval from shareholders and the fund’s board.
